Beyond Static Personas: Situational Personality Steering for Large Language Models

Zesheng Wei ††thanks: Work was done during a visit at SMU. Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China Email: ydeng@smu.edu.sg    Mengxiang Li Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Zilei Wang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China    Yang Deng Affiliation: Singapore Management University{zswei, mxli02}@mail.ustc.edu.cn, zlwang@ustc.edu.cn
Abstract

Personalized Large Language Models (LLMs) facilitate more natural, human-like interactions in human-centric applications. However, existing personalization methods are constrained by limited controllability and high resource demands. Furthermore, their reliance on static personality modeling restricts adaptability across varying situations. To address these limitations, we first demonstrate the existence of situation-dependency and consistent situation-behavior patterns within LLM personalities through a multi-perspective analysis of persona neurons. Building on these insights, we propose IRiS, a training-free, neuron-based Identify-Retrieve-Steer framework for advanced situational personality steering. Our approach comprises situational persona neuron identification, situation-aware neuron retrieval, and similarity-weighted steering. We empirically validate our framework on PersonalityBench and our newly introduced SPBench, a comprehensive situational personality benchmark. Experimental results show that our method surpasses best-performing baselines, demonstrating IRiS’s generalization and robustness to complex, unseen situations and different models architecture.

1 Introduction

“Behavior is a function of the person and their environment.” (Lewin, 2013)

— Kurt Lewin

The advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has catalyzed a wide range of human-centric applications such as role-playing (Chen et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2025a), personalized assistance (Deng et al., 2024b; Mok et al., 2025), user simulation (Zhang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025), and social simulation (Chen et al., 2024b; Zhou et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). These applications require models to express coherent personalities while adapting their behavior across diverse interaction situations, making personality modeling a central challenge for LLM personalization. However, most existing approaches implicitly assume that behavior is determined solely by stable personality traits. This assumption conflicts with a core principle in psychology: behavior is a function of both the person and the environment Lewin (2013). When situational factors are ignored, personalized agents may exhibit superficial consistency yet fail to respond appropriately across varying situations.

Existing approaches to endowing LLMs with personality are primarily categorized into training-based and training-free methods. Training-based methods rely on large-scale, high-quality datasets to align models with specific personalized preferences (Li et al., 2025), utilizing techniques such as Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) (Wang et al., 2025b; Tan et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024b) or Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Li et al., 2024a). While effective, these methods are computationally expensive (Szep et al., 2025) and difficult to adapt post hoc (Tseng et al., 2024). Training-free methods, including prompt-based personalization (Jiang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023) and direct internal steering (Deng et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2025), offer greater flexibility but suffer from instability, limited controllability, and weak theoretical grounding. Although prompt-based methods can incorporate conversational history as situational context, they treat it merely as a "black-box" input. Relying on implicit attention mechanisms for this modulation lacks transparency, often causing unstable personality expression. Crucially, both training and training-free paradigms lack a mechanistic framework to explicitly model the underlying persona-situation interactions.

In contrast to the static assumptions underlying existing LLM personalization methods, personality psychology provides a well-established persona-situation interactional account of behavior Lewin (2013). While early trait theories assume cross-situational consistency (Newcomb, 1929; Allport, 1937), subsequent work demonstrates that stable traits alone are insufficient to explain behavior across diverse situations (Mischel, 1968; Mischel and Peake, 1982). In particular, the Cognitive-Affective Personality System (CAPS) theory (Mischel and Shoda, 1995) argues that human behavior varies across diverse situations. Empirical studies further demonstrate that different situations selectively activate cognitive and affective units (Mischel et al., 2002), and that personality coherence is expressed through consistent situation-behavior patterns (Ayduk and Gyurak, 2008). To date, these persona-situation interactional mechanisms have not been systematically investigated or integrated into LLM-based personalization.

Motivated by the above psychology studies, we first empirically examine whether LLMs exhibit human-like situational dependency and consistent situation-behavior personality patterns, through multi-perspective analysis of internal neurons. As illustrated in Figure 1, our preliminary results show that the maximum PCA distance between situational topics within a single domain is comparable to the distance observed between distinct personality domains, suggesting that situational variation can induce significant personality-level representational shifts. Building on this observation, we propose a training-free, neuron-based Identify-Retrieve-Steer framework for situational personality steering, named IRiS. The framework first identifies situational persona neurons from a set of historical situations, which serve as instructive priors. Given a novel situational situation, IRiS estimates its similarity to these historical situations, retrieves the corresponding persona neurons, and applies coefficient-weighted steering to enable precise and situation-aware personalization.

Comprehensive evaluations across two personality benchmarks validate the SOTA performance of IRiS, demonstrating effective generalization to unseen situations and robustness within complex situations. Furthermore, extensive experiments verify the adaptability of our approach across diverse model architectures. To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We empirically validate human-like situational dependency and consistent situation-behavior personality patterns within LLMs, pioneering the integration of these psychological mechanisms to guide precise personality steering.

  • •

    We propose the IRiS framework, a psychology-grounded approach that leverages instructive priors for situational-aware retrieval and steering.

  • •

    We conduct extensive experiments and in-depth analyses to verify our framework’s effectiveness, offering intuitive insights into situational personality for future research and applications.

2 Preliminary Analysis

The preliminary analysis aims to investigate the situational impact on LLMs’ personality manifestation, and to validate the theory of situation-behavior consistency within LLMs.

2.1 Backgrounds

Personality Model

In this work, we adopt the widely validated Big-Five model (Tupes and Christal, 1992) as the foundational personality framework, which comprises five domains: openness (O), conscientiousness (C), extroversion (E), agreeableness (A), and neuroticism (N). Each domain encompasses opposing aspects (e.g., extraverted versus introverted within the E domain).

Neurons in LLMs

Modern LLMs adopt the auto-regressive transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) architecture, which consists of L stacked transformer blocks. Previous work has shown that knowledge, such as personality, is stored in specific neurons within the feed-forward networks (FFNs) of each block (Dai et al., 2022). Specifically, in layer ll, given input XlX^{l} for a token, we have:

FFN​(Xl)=act​(Xl​W1l)​W2l\text{FFN}(X^{l})=\text{act}(X^{l}W^{l}_{1})W^{l}_{2} (1)

where Xl∈ℝdX^{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, W1l∈ℝd×dhW^{l}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{h}}, W2l∈ℝdh×dW^{l}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times d}, and a​c​tact represents the activation function (e.g., ReLU (Agarap, 2019)). More recent advanced LLMs (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025) have replaced the ReLU non-linearity with the GLU (Shazeer, 2020) activation function to achieve better performance:

FFN’​(Xl)=(act​(Xl​W1l)⊙(Xl​W3l))​W2l\text{FFN'}(X^{l})=(\text{act}(X^{l}W^{l}_{1})\odot(X^{l}W^{l}_{3}))W^{l}_{2} (2)

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication, and W3l∈ℝd×dhW^{l}_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{h}} is the gating weight matrix.

In layer ll, the it​hi^{th} neuron can be conceptualized as applying a linear transformation to column ii of W1lW^{l}_{1} followed by the non-linear activation. The activation value of a neuron is positively correlated with the expression of corresponding facts. In this context, a neuron is considered activated if its activation value exceeds zero (Nair and Hinton, 2010).

Neuron Identification Dataset & Situational Topic Category

To identify persona neurons within LLMs, we employ the dataset from PersonalityBench (Deng et al., 2024a), denoted as 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, which comprises a diverse set of descriptive personalization prompts and situational questions designed to elicit personality-driven responses. To investigate the influence of varying situations on LLMs’ personality, these questions are categorized into MM = 30 distinct topics, following the taxonomy of UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023). Further details are provided in Appendix A.

2.2 Empirical Study

The targets of our analysis are situational persona neurons in LLMs, which are identified by measuring activation differences of neurons within LLMs under contrastive personality prompts within situational topics, with detailed explanations in section 3.1.

2.2.1 Situational Impact on LLMs’ Personality

We analyze the activation states and layer-wise distribution of persona neurons to investigate situation impact on LLMs’ personality. Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) are adopted as target LLMs for validation. Comprehensive results are provided in Appendix C.

Activation-Level Perspective

We collect the activation probabilities of all situational persona neurons across diverse topics. For comparison, we also derive "global persona neurons" by disregarding topic distinctions, establishing a baseline for cross-situational consistency. We then perform Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the feature vectors vf∈ℝL×dhv_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{h}}, which are constructed by populating the activation probability values of specific neurons while setting irrelevant neurons’ positions to zero. As illustrated in Figure 1 (Qwen) and Figure 5 (Llama), situational persona neurons exhibit significant variation across topics. Notably, the maximum Euclidean distance between topics within a single domain in the PCA space is comparable to the distance between distinct personality domains. Moreover, nearby points in the PCA space correspond to semantically similar topics, confirming that the observed variation is systematic rather than noise. Given the independence of Big Five personality domains (Goldberg, 2013), this result indicates that distinct situations induces personality-level representational shifts in LLMs.

Layer-Level Perspective

We further investigate the variations in the count and proportion of situational personality neurons across diverse topics among all layers. For illustrative clarity, we select eight topics and eight layers spanning the early, middle, and late stages within personality domain C. As shown in Figure 2(a), within a specific personality domain, questions involving different situational topics significantly influence the distribution of neurons controlling LLM personality. Similarly, as illustrated in Figure 2(b), the proportion of situational persona neurons per layer exhibits significant disparity, with a maximum difference of 2.23% observed in layer 16. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the middle layers contain the highest concentration of persona neurons across all topics, which aligns with findings from prior studies (Skean et al., 2025; Liu and Niehues, 2025).

2.2.2 Stability of Situation-Behavior in LLMs

We next investigate human-like personality patterns of situation-behavior consistency in LLMs. We hypothesize that analogous situations elicit consistent activation patterns in persona neurons, thereby generating coherent personalized behaviors. To investigate this, we select four topics within a specific personality domain, each comprising 1,200 questions covering both aspect. Feature vectors are constructed by aggregating the activation probabilities of situational persona neurons across output tokens, following the methodology in section 2.2.1. Given the high dimensionality and substantial sample size of vectors, we apply Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) following PCA. As illustrated in Figure 2(c), instances from the same topic form distinct and cohesive clusters, suggesting that diverse questions within a situation elicit convergent internal activations. Notably, overlaps between certain clusters reflect semantic correlations across questions, indicating that these representations exist within a continuous latent space rather than being strictly binary.

3 IRiS Framework

Empirical study in section 2.2 has shown the distinct activation patterns to exert personalized control across different situations and the principle of situation-behavior stability within LLMs. Based on this empirical conclusion, we propose a human-like train-free Identify-Retrieve-Steer (IRiS) framework to achieve more accurate personality steering. As illustrated in Figure 3, our framework operates in three stages: (1) identifying situational persona neurons (section 3.1); (2) retrieving relevant historical topics via a situation-aware module (section 3.2); and (3) modulating the model’s personality in novel situation using similarity-weighted steering (section 3.3). To facilitate consistency throughout the paper, we summarize the mathematical notations in appendix B.

3.1 Identifying Situational Persona Neurons

Given a personality domain 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we employ both positive and negative personality prompt to instruct the target LLM to respond to the set of situational questions 𝒬𝒟t\mathcal{Q}_{\mathcal{D}}^{t} regarding topic tt. We then calculate the activation probability for all neurons across all output tokens. Specifically, the activation probability of the it​hi^{th} neuron in layer ll is computed as:

Pi,ls=𝔼[𝕀(act(Xl(W1l)i)>0)∣𝒟s,t]P_{i,l}^{s}=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{I}\left(\text{act}\left(X^{l}(W^{l}_{1})_{i}\right)>0\right)\mid{\mathcal{D}}^{s},t\right] (3)

Where 𝕀⁡(CLOSE\mathbb{I}(·)) is the indicator function and s∈{+,−}s\in\{+,-\} represents the personality aspect. To eliminate impact from irrelevant content and locate the persona neurons, we compute the activation difference across all neurons between positive and negative traits, defined as Δ​P=P+−P−\Delta P=P^{+}-P^{-}. We classify all neurons, termed situational persona neurons, into positive (Nt𝒟+N^{\mathcal{D}^{+}}_{t}), negative (Nt𝒟−N^{\mathcal{D}^{-}}_{t}), or irrelevant (NtIN^{I}_{t}) for specific topic t{t} based on whether their activation difference Δ​P\Delta P is greater than a threshold 10%10\%, less than −10%-10\%, or falls between these bounds, respectively. For all personality domain and its corresponding topic, we store both NT𝒟+N^{\mathcal{D}^{+}}_{T} and NT𝒟−N^{\mathcal{D}^{-}}_{T} with the location, historical activation value, raw activation probability of its aspect, and activation probability difference in Situational Persona Neurons Bank, Where 𝒟∈{O,C,E,A,N}\mathcal{D}\in\{O,C,E,A,N\}, and TT is the topic set.

3.2 Situation-aware Neurons Retrieval

We have established that LLMs utilize highly consistent persona neurons to regulate personality expression across similar situations in section 2.2.2. Consequently, when the model encounters a novel situation, retrieving and adjusting situational persona neurons associated with similar contexts can yield precise personality control. Specifically, given a novel, topic-agnostic question and a target personality domain 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we firstly compute the activation difference vector Δ​v\Delta v between the positive and negative aspects (same as the subtraction operation in section 3.1). Secondly, for neuron belonging to 𝒟\mathcal{D} and specific topic tt, we construct the feature vectors vt𝒟∈ℝL×dhv^{\mathcal{D}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d_{h}} using the raw activation probability values across positive and negative neurons, while setting irrelevant neurons’ position to zero. We then compute the cosine similarity score between Δ​v\Delta v with vt𝒟v^{\mathcal{D}}_{t} across all topics in TT:

Sim​(vt𝒟,Δ​𝐯)=vt𝒟⋅Δ​𝐯‖vt𝒟‖⋅‖Δ​𝐯‖t∈T\text{Sim}(v^{\mathcal{D}}_{t},\Delta\mathbf{v})=\frac{v^{\mathcal{D}}_{t}\cdot\Delta\mathbf{v}}{\|v^{\mathcal{D}}_{t}\|\cdot\|\Delta\mathbf{v}\|}\quad t\in T (4)

To effectively accentuate the distinctions between scores, we apply a softmax function on all similarity scores, obtaining the normalized situation similarity coefficients ete_{t} for each topic tt:

et=Softmax​(Sim​(vt𝒟,Δ​𝐯))t∈Te_{t}=\text{Softmax}\left(\text{Sim}(v^{\mathcal{D}}_{t},\Delta\mathbf{v})\right)\quad t\in T (5)

3.3 Situational Personality Steering

The soft situation similarity coefficients quantify the semantic alignment between the current situation and reference situations. Motivated by the multi-contextual nuances of questions in 𝒬\mathcal{Q} identified in section 2.2.2, we evaluate the precision of these coefficients in Appendix E. The demonstrated high accuracy validates the reliability of this semantic alignment, enabling nuanced, situational personality steering that remains robust even in complex multi-contextual scenarios. Building on this validation, for a target personality aspect 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we amplify the activation of situational persona neurons via coefficient-weighted modulation, ensuring the intervention is proportional to situational relevance:

n′=nori+∑t∈Tet⋅γ⋅a95⋅f⁡(Δ​P),if ​n∈Nt𝒟+n^{\prime}=n_{\text{ori}}+\sum\nolimits_{t\in T}e_{t}\cdot\gamma\cdot a_{\text{95}}\cdot f(\Delta P),\quad\text{if }n\in N^{\mathcal{D}^{+}}_{t} (6)

Where norin_{\text{ori}} represents the original activation, γ\gamma is to control the magnitude of adjustment, and a95a_{95} represents the 95t​h95^{th} percentile of historical activation value of this neuron to constrain modification. Activation differences are also accounted for by applying a softmax-based smoothing function, defined as f⁡(x)=11+e−10⋅(|x|−0.15){f(x)}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-10\cdot(|x|-0.15)}}, to the value. we introduce a threshold σ\sigma and deactivate those negative situational persona neurons with corresponding similarity coefficients greater than σ\sigma:

n′=min(0,nori),if n∈⋃t:et>σNt𝒟−n^{\prime}=\min(0,n_{\text{ori}}),\quad\text{if }n\in\bigcup\nolimits_{t:e_{t}>\sigma}N^{\mathcal{D}^{-}}_{t} (7)

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarking Dataset.  We employ test set from PersonalityBench (Deng et al., 2024a) . Notably, these situational questions lack explicit situation labels, whose categories may fall outside the topic set TT. We introduce the Situational Personality Benchmark (SPBench) as a supplementary test set comprising 90 situational questions per personality domain distributed across 30 topic categories, with construction detail and intrinsic evaluations provided in Appendix F and  G.1. Such settings guarantee the assessment on both generalization to unseen situational situation, and the robustness in comprehensive benchmark.

Evaluation Metrics.  We evaluate personality expression (mean), stability (variance), and response fluency using a 5-point LLM-as-a-Judge scale. Higher scores indicate stronger trait presence or fluency quality. Thus, personality scores for negative aspects are inverted using (6−score)(6-\text{score}). For each personality domain, we report the results by summing its positive and negative aspect scores.

Baselines.  We adopt a diverse range of LLM personalization baselines covering both inference-time and training-time alignment. These include prompt-based methods (Simple Prompt (SP), P2P^{2} (Jiang et al., 2023)), direct steering methods (ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024), NPTI (Deng et al., 2024a)), and Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) using LoRA (Hu et al., 2021), serving as upper bound for reference purpose. Details of implementing these baselines are presented in Appendix D.

Implementation Details.  To ensure a fair comparison, we maintain consistent γ\gamma values for both IRiS and NPTI (1.4 for PersonalityBench and 1.1 for SPBench). LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations are conducted using the gpt-4o-20240806 (Hurst et al., 2024) API with greedy decoding. With the exception of section 5.3, Llama-3-8B-Instruct serves as the target LLM throughout section 4 and section 5.

4.2 Experimental Results

Results on PersonalityBench   As shown in Table 1, SP achieves optimal performance on A domain, while exhibiting significant deficiencies regarding N and O. These results underscore the inherent instability of prompt-based methods as previously discussed in section 1. In contrast, IRiS outperforms all baselines in terms of mean and variance of personality performance scores for E, N, O, the overall average across all traits (m​e​a​n=9.59,v​a​r​i​a​n​c​e=0.30)\left(mean=9.59,variance=0.30\right), and score variance on C domain. By surpassing all direct steering baselines, our approach demonstrates more precise neuron control, enabling the model to exhibit personality with greater accuracy and consistency. Furthermore, IRiS achieves performance marginally below the SFT baseline while remaining train-free. These superior results demonstrate our framework’s resource efficiency, controllability, and generalization to unseen situational situations. Fluency scores are analyzed in Appendix H.

Results on SPBench  Notably, PersonalityBench is a relatively simple benchmark where baseline performances saturate near theoretical maximums. While SPBench matches its per-domain question count, it offers a more challenging standard by covering a broader range of situations. As shown in Table 2, IRiS consistently outperforms all baselines on average, underscoring its robustness in navigating complex scenarios. Furthermore, several baselines suffer performance degradation in specific personality domains within SPBench. This suggests that existing methods struggle with personality control in complex situations, further validating SPBench as a comprehensive benchmark.

5 Further Analysis

5.1 Human Evaluation

We recruit five human evaluators to rank the responses from four top-performing methods. We conduct a pre-evaluation training for all human evaluators and verify their inter-annotator agreement, with more details provided in Appendix G.2. We aggregate the evaluation results to calculate both the distribution of rankings across all methods and the overall average ranks, as presented in Table 3. The results demonstrate that IRiS achieves the highest proportion of first-place rankings and the most favorable average rank. These findings are consistent with the outcomes of the LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, further validating the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

5.2 Effect of Hyperparameters

Impact of γ\gamma  The parameter γ\gamma in Eq. 6 regulates the steering magnitude of activation values for positive persona neurons. We investigate its impact on overall personality performance scores by conducting an ablation study with values ranging from 0.9 to 1.5 across two test sets. As illustrated in Figure 4(a) and Figure 4(b), both IRiS and NPTI underperform compared to P2P^{2} at lower γ\gamma values, primarily constrained by their preset prompt. However, performance improves for both methods as γ\gamma increases. Notably, our method consistently outperforms NPTI. For instance, our approach at γ=1.3\gamma=1.3 surpasses NPTI at γ=1.4\gamma=1.4. These results validate that our framework outperforms baselines by leveraging precise neuron modification to achieve superior efficiency and accuracy in personality elicitation under identical hyperparameter settings.

Impact of σ\sigma  The parameter σ\sigma in Eq. 7 governs the selection threshold for negative neurons. A smaller σ\sigma implies a larger number of negative neurons are selected for deactivation. To investigate this, we conducted an ablation study on σ\sigma on the PersonalityBench , while keeping other hyper-parameters fixed. We evaluated four candidate values: {0.01,0.05,0.10,0.20}\{0.01,0.05,0.10,0.20\}, analyzing their impact on both personality performance and fluency of results on positive aspect of A domain. As shown in Figure 4(c), both the personality performance score and variance exhibit an initial increase followed by a decline as σ\sigma increases. Conversely, Figure 4(d) illustrates the results for response fluency: as σ\sigma increases, fewer negative neurons are deactivated, leading to improved generation fluency. Consequently, we set σ=0.10\sigma=0.10 given the stable fluency between 0.10 and 0.20.

5.3 Generalizability Across Different Models

To evaluate the robustness of our method across different LLMs, we extend our experiments to include two additional advanced models: Qwen3-8B and gemma-3-12B-it (Team et al., 2025). These models introduce architectural diversity. Specifically, Qwen utilizes the SiLU (Elfwing et al., 2017) activation function, consistent with our primary model Llama-3-8B-Instruct, while Gemma employs GeLU (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2023). We maintain constant hyperparameters across all settings, with the exception of γ\gamma, which is adjusted to 1.01.0 for Qwen and 1.31.3 for Gemma. As illustrated in Figure 4, IRiS ranks first in the majority of personality domains and second in the remainder, achieving the best overall performance on both models. These results demonstrate the robustness of our approach across varying model architectures.

5.4 Impact of Model Scaling on Generalizability

To investigate the scalability and consistency of our method across varying model sizes, we conduct a scaling analysis utilizing different scales within the Qwen3 family, specifically Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B. All hyperparameters are kept strictly constant across these models. As presented in Table 5, existing methods exhibit noticeable scaling inconsistencies, where increasing model parameters does not guarantee proportional performance gains. Notably, scaling up the model size can occasionally result in performance degradation. For instance, baseline methods (e.g., P2P^{2} and NPTI) on the 8B model unexpectedly outperform their 14B counterparts in the C domain. In contrast, IRiS demonstrates highly robust scalability. As the model parameters increase, our method not only steadily improves in average performance but also significantly reduces variance (from 0.25 on 0.6B to 0.06 on 14B). Furthermore, IRiS consistently maintains SOTA overall performance across all three scales. These findings strongly validate the reliability and effectiveness of our approach, proving its capability to harness the power of larger models stably without suffering from prompt sensitivity.

5.5 Inherent Situational Impact on Personality Expression

Situational factors inherently influence the expression of personality. To investigate this nuanced impact, we collect results from IRiS on SPBench and calculate a standardized score for each topic. Specifically, the raw scores for the positive and negative aspects are independently standardized by subtracting their respective means and dividing by their standard deviations. These standardized values are then averaged to derive the final score for each topic. This metric quantifies the directional impact of a topic, where higher values indicate a positive deviation. Table 6 shows the topics exhibiting the most significant deviations across all domains. Notably, "History and Nostalgia" yields a strongly negative score in Neuroticism, suggesting that factual topics inherently suppress Neuroticism by eliciting calmer responses, thereby attenuating the effect of the intended persona adjustment. Qualitative case studies are provided in Appendix K to explicitly reveal the distinct characteristics of situational impact on the responses steered by IRiS.

6 Related Works

Early training-based LLM personalization approaches rely on large-scale data to align models with general human preferences (Longpre et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b). While subsequent research addresses granularity limitations by leveraging fine-grained datasets (Bu et al., 2025) or training user-specific LoRA modules (Tan et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025d), these methods incur significant computational overhead, necessitate complex data curation, and lack the flexibility to adapt to evolving user preferences. Alternatively, training-free strategies employ contextual guidance, ranging from explicit prompting (Tan et al., 2024a; Zhu et al., 2025) to implicit mechanisms such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation for accessing personalized content (Richardson et al., 2023; Salemi et al., 2024). Although flexible, these approaches are often unstable due to their sensitivity to provided context quality. Another training-free paradigm involves direct internal steering, such as editing attention heads (Zhu et al., 2025), perturbing hidden states among layers via probing classifiers (Ju et al., 2025), or modifying personality-related neuron activations (Deng et al., 2024a). However, these interventions typically lack robust psychological grounding, treating personality as a static attribute, which fail to capture the dynamic nature of human behavior across varying situations.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduce IRiS, a neuron-based situational personality steering framework in LLMs. Grounded in our validation of situational dependency and consistent situation-behavior patterns within LLMs, IRiS integrates psychological theory with mechanistic intervention to achieve precise and human-like personality steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IRiS significantly outperforms existing paradigms on two comprehensive benchmarks and exhibits robust generalization across different model architectures. Furthermore, our in-depth analysis provides valuable insights to guide future research in this domain.

Limitations

We discuss the limitations from two perspectives:

Trade-offs Between Personalization and Instruction Following Capabilities

Our case studies reveal that steering models toward specific personality traits can occasionally compromise instruction following, which is a common issue in LLM personalization approaches (Handa et al., 2025; de Araujo et al., 2025). For instance, inducing the negative aspect of Openness may cause the model to refuse interaction, reflecting realistic "closed" human behaviors. This highlights an inherent trade-off between personality expression and task completion. Given the diverse applications of LLM personalization, this balance requires scenario-specific consideration. We also conduct comprehensive discussion on this issue, including evaluations of response fluency (Appendix H) and general instruction-following capabilities (Appendix I).

Granularity of Situation Topics

A second limitation lies in the granularity of our retrieval mechanism, which currently relies on a taxonomy of 30 historical reference topics from Ding et al. (2023). The fixed segmentation may be insufficient for certain nuances, underscoring the need for more open-ended situational modeling. Nevertheless, our framework effectively retrieves multiple relevant situations based on current unseen situational question. Furthermore, the superior performance across two benchmarks, and in-depth analysis in section 3.3 and appendix E demonstrate IRiS’s efficiency and robustness to unseen complex situations.

Ethical Considerations

We strictly adhere to the licensing terms of the models utilized in this study. Llama-3-8B-Instruct is governed by the Meta Llama 3 Community License Agreement11 1 https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct/blob/main/LICENSE, Qwen3-8B is distributed under the Apache License Version 2.022 2 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B/blob/main/LICENSE, and gemma-3-12b-it is subject to the Gemma Terms of Use33 3 https://ai.google.dev/gemma/terms. Additionally, the Roberta-large employed for the verification experiments in appendix E operates under the MIT License. We have properly cited all software, datasets, and models used, and we affirm that all presented results are intended exclusively for scientific research purposes. Our proposed benchmarking dataset SPBench consists of synthetic LLM-generated questions. It contains no personally identifiable information, such as names or individual identifiers, nor does it include offensive content.

Appendix

Appendix A Situational Topics Set

Figure 8 presents the complete situational topics set used in this paper defined in UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023). This set comprises 30 comprehensive categories covering various aspects of daily life, facilitating the investigation of personality manifestations and mechanisms across diverse situations.

Appendix B Notations

Appendix C Comprehensive Empirical Study

C.1 PCA Analysis of Persona neurons

We report the complete results of PCA on the activation patterns of situational and global persona neurons. To demonstrate the universality of our findings across different models, we selected Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B as our target LLMs. As illustrated in Figure 6, situational persona neurons within the same personality domain exhibit significant variance. Notably, the maximum PCA distance between these neurons within certain domain is of the same order of magnitude as the distance between distinct, highly independent personalities. Furthermore, we mark two most prominent personality domains in Qwen model for detailed analysis, as shown in Figure 1. Following the format of Figure 5, we annotate two proximal topic points within these personality for reference.

C.2 Layer Analysis of Persona Neurons

We present the comprehensive analysis of the situational persona neurons across all layers and diverse topics, with the authentic counts and proportions illustrated in Figure 7 and Figure 8, respectively. These results characterize the variability of persona neurons associated with traits of specific personality domain when subjected to different situations. Furthermore, both figures clearly illustrate the distribution of these neurons across the models, revealing that the neurons governing personality expression are most densely concentrated in the middle and final layers of the models.

Appendix D Implementation Details of Baselines

As for the baselines of personalization methods within LLMs, we choose the followings studied in our experiments. All experiments are conducted on a server equipped with 4×\times NVIDIA L40S GPUs.

Simple Prompt: This method explicitly defines personality by adapting trait descriptors directly into the system prompt (e.g., "You are an extraverted person"). This instructs the model to align its generated response with the target trait.

P2P^{2} (Jiang et al., 2023): This approach leverages comprehensive descriptions of personality traits to provide richer semantic constraints. P2P^{2} thus induces more consistent and verifiable personified behaviors across diverse situational queries and open-ended tasks.

ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024): ActAdd is an inference-time intervention that applies vector addition to the Transformer’s residual stream to steer high-level attributes, specifically personality traits in our experiments. Following authentic methodology, we adopt grid search to determine the optimal hyperparameters for each personality domain. The prompts used to calculate the steering vector are consistent with those employed during the Identify stage in IRiS.

Supervised Fine-Tuning: This baseline enables the model to internalize target personality traits at the parameter level, typically yielding the most robust and stable behavioral expression. Since it directly modifies model weights rather than relying on prompting or inference-time intervention, this method serves as the "training-based upper bound" for reference purpose. Specifically, we collect all responses generated during the Identify stage as ground truth data. To ensure specialized adaptation, we train a distinct LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) adapter for each personality aspect, targeting all linear modules with a standard cross-entropy loss. The model is trained using BF16 precision with a maximum sequence length of 4096. Optimization hyperparameters include a learning rate of 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}, a LoRA rank of 8 (α=16\alpha=16), and a per-device batch size of 8. Training for each personality aspect requires approximately 3 GPU hours.

Appendix E Accuracy Analysis for Soft Situation Similarity Coefficients

To establish a semantic ground truth, we fine-tune RoBERTa-Large44 4 https://huggingface.co/FacebookAI/xlm-roberta-large (325M) (Liu et al., 2019) for each personality domain using all questions paired with single-label situational topics in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, employing a 30-dimensional MLP classifier. The resulting softmax probability distributions serve as the reference standard for evaluating the Top-2, Top-5, and Top-8 accuracy of our soft situation similarity coefficients. Our approach demonstrates robust performance across all domains in this 30-class classification task. As shown in Table 9, for the Openness domain, we achieve a Top-2 accuracy of 27.2% and a Top-8 accuracy of 63.3%. Considering the inherent misalignment between RoBERTa’s and neuron-level semantic space, these results are sufficient to validate that the soft situation similarity coefficients retrieved in section 3.2 effectively capture the granular situational semantics embedded in the questions. Notably, our method achieves this in a completely training-free manner.

Appendix F Construction Details of SPBench

We follow the methodology to generate situational questions as PersonalityBench (Deng et al., 2024a). For a given personality domain and situational topic, we randomly select a descriptive facet as defined by the Five-Factor Model (McCrae and John, 1992). Example facets for each personality domain are presented in Table 14. Utilizing these facets, we instruct GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) to generate situational questions via one-shot prompting. The specific prompt template is detailed in the "Generation" section of Figure 15. Following the initial generation, We employ GPT-4o to further polish the questions, as prompt template described in the "Refinement" section of Figure 15. We generate three situational questions per topic within each personality domain, resulting in a total of 450 questions (90 questions across 5 personality domains). These questions are designed to be neutral and applicable to both positive and negative personality domains. By incorporating a diverse and balanced array of situational topics, SPBench serves as a more comprehensive benchmark for evaluation.

Appendix G Evaluation Details

G.1 Intrinsic Evaluation of SPBench

To validate the quality of SPBench, we conduct a comprehensive intrinsic evaluation focusing on two key metrics: Inducement Validity (IV) and Situational Authenticity (SA), both scored on a scale of 1 to 10. IV measures the efficacy of a situational question in activating a target personality trait, thereby prompting the model to exhibit that trait in its response. SA evaluates the realism of the scenario description, ensuring alignment with real-world plausibility. We employ both LLM-as-a-Judge approach and human evaluation for comprehensive assessment. For the automatic evaluation, to mitigate potential self-preference bias from the source model, we utilize the claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 API with greedy decoding. For the human evaluation, we hire five graduate students specializing in psychology. Prior to assessment, evaluators undergo rigorous training with manually verified examples to ensure alignment with metric definitions. The criteria provided to human evaluators are identical to those used in the automatic evaluation. Each evaluator assesses situational questions (55 personality domains ×90\times 90 items), and their scores are averaged to produce the final reported results. The evaluation was conducted over two days, with seven-hour daily sessions (08:00 to 17:00, excluding breaks). Evaluators were compensated at a rate of $0.30 per question. Results are shown in Table 10, SPBench demonstrates superior quality across both metrics. Average scores for each personality domain are consistently high, with IV reaching 8.33 (automatic) and 8.85 (human), and SA averaging approximately 8.0. These results underscore the robustness and reliability of SPBench as a comprehensive benchmark for personality evaluation.

G.2 Ranking Across Different Methods

To conduct a human evaluation of the generated responses, we recruit five graduate students specializing in psychology as the human evaluators. The evaluation dataset consisted of 300 response samples across all personality aspects (30 randomly selected samples per aspect) of the PersonalityBench test set, comprising responses from four top-performing experimental settings: SP, P2P^{2}, NPTI, and IRiS. Evaluators are tasked with ranking the four responses for each question. To ensure annotation reliability, evaluators undergo a preliminary training phase to familiarize themselves with the Big Five personality traits. Specifically, they first complete the Big Five Inventory (John et al., 1991) to internalize the domain definitions, followed by a review of the descriptive facets in the Five-Factor Model (McCrae and John, 1992) to enhance understanding of all personality domains. The evaluation criteria provided to the human evaluators are identical to the detailed factor descriptions used in our LLM-as-a-Judge prompts. Prior to the formal evaluation, we conduct a pilot study under identical settings, yielding a relatively high mean pair-wise agreement of 72.5%. The assessment is conducted via a custom interface developed with Gradio55 5 https://github.com/gradio-app/gradio, which displays the situational question alongside the four generated responses, shown in Figure 9. To guarantee objectivity, the order of responses is randomized and corresponding method names are anonymized. Following the evaluation, rankings are aggregated and statistically analyzed. The evaluators’ working hours are consistent with those described in section G.1. Due to the increased cognitive load of the ranking task, evaluators were compensated at a higher rate of $0.50 per response set upon completion.

Appendix H Experimental Results of Fluency Score

Figure 11 presents the fluency scores for all methods evaluated on PersonalityBench. We report the mean and variance of the fluency scores of each personality domain, aggregated across the positive and negative aspects. To ensure a fair comparison, we adopt the γ\gamma value selection strategy for positive neuron modification used in NPTI (Deng et al., 2024a) and maintain consistency across all hyperparameters. Our method outperforms NPTI, another representative neuron-based personalization method, across the A, E, N, and O domains, as well as in overall average fluency. These results demonstrate the superior precision of persona neuron localization and the efficacy of IRiS.

Appendix I Evaluation of General Capabilities

To assess the impact of IRiS on general instruction-following capabilities, we utilize the GSM8K66 6 https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/gsm8k (Cobbe et al., 2021) and CommonsenseQA77 7 https://huggingface.co/datasets/tau/commonsense_qa (Talmor et al., 2019) benchmarks. We evaluate Llama-3-8B-Instruct using IRiS across all personality domains, adhering to the experimental settings reported in the official Llama-3 documentation (Grattafiori et al., 2024). Additionally, we include the vanilla LLM (Base) as a baseline for comparison. The results are presented in Table 12, with results that outperform the base setting highlighted in bold. IRiS exhibits a marginal decline compared to the vanilla setting across most personality aspects, which means it maintains robust general instruction-following capabilities. Notably, we observe performance improvements in specific aspects. Through a detailed case study, we attribute these improvements to two factors: (1) given that both benchmarks incorporate real-world scenarios, editing relevant situational persona neurons enhances the model’s contextual understanding, thereby improving problem comprehension; and (2) steering specific personality aspects encourages more detailed explanations, facilitating deeper reasoning through extended generation.

Appendix J Latency Analysis

We calculated the total computational cost by aggregating all samples used across the training/search and testing phases. The average latency per sample for each experimental setting is presented in Table 13. Our approach achieves a reduction of 0.16s per sample in the initial phase compared to training-based methods, albeit with a marginal increase in inference time during the testing stage.

Appendix K Comprehensive Case Study

We present a comprehensive comparative case study of responses generated by SP, NPTI, and our method across all personality domains. Detailed analyses are provided in Figure 17 (A), Figure 18 (C), Figure 19 (E), Figure 20 (N), and Figure 21 (O). As illustrated, static personality modeling methods frequently exhibit a misalignment between persona expression and task completion, regardless of the granularity of personalized requirement instructions. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the negative poles of personality traits. Taking the creative fairy tale writing task in Figure 21 as an example, the SP and NPTI baselines initially signal reluctance (e.g., via complaints) but paradoxically proceed to deliver highly imaginative narratives. This creates a distinct dissonance where the persona contradicts the actual task performance, exposing the inherent limitations of conceptualizing personality as a static, cross-situation consistent trait, as discussed in section 1. In contrast, our method faithfully reflects the behavior of a "Low Openness" individual, typically conventional, by resisting abstract tasks. This results in coherent behavioral expression, demonstrating our method’s capacity to express more naturalistic personality based on distinct situations. Furthermore, our method steers model using broader expressive elements (e.g., colloquialisms, slang, and emojis like to signify aspiration) to convey nuanced emotional states without our explicit prompting, which are rarely observed in other baselines.
